To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

“early childhood intervention can have a positive impact on later cognitive and academic performance, but that this impact is highly variable and that a variety of individual and family factors may be associated with outcome status” (p. 3).

“children with developmental disabilities who participated in ECSE programs at the preschool level had better academic performance in the 8th grade than would have been expected on the basis of their preschool cognitive performance, but the extent of the improvement varied substantially.

the cognitive and academic outcomes of children with disabilities are highly heterogeneous, that there are numerous individual and family factors that are associated with outcome status, that there is no simple way to predict outcome status, and that, in spite of these facts, there is much to learn about the processes that lead to positive or negative outcomes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of children with disabilities and the prediction of their later performance.
the long-term effects of preschool intervention on cognitive and academic development.
the long-term effects of ECSE.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the children who had been in ECSE were, on average, doing well, and that there were many factors, both personal and contextual, that were associated with their later performance.
ECSE is not effective for all children, but it is effective for many, and it is not ineffective for most. (Contains 3 tables and 1 figure.)
the children who had participated in the ECSE programs were, on the whole, functioning at a level comparable to that of children who had not participated in ECSE.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cognitive status of a child with a disability at the time of ECSE enrollment is an important but not a sufficient predictor of later academic status.

, although the cognitive status of children at age 3 is the strongest predictor of their academic performance 10 years later, other factors also play an important role in determining the long-term outcome of children who have been served in ECSE programs.

children who were referred to ECSE for gross motor concerns but not social concerns and whose temperament was positive were likely to be academic improvers, whereas those who were referred for social concerns and whose temperaments were negative were likely to be decreasers.
The main takeaway from our work is that
early intervention programs should be designed to provide children and their parents with a range of supports and interventions that will enable them to meet their own goals for their child.
early identification of risk and early intervention are not sufficient to predict long-term outcomes.
, although preschool cognitive ability is a powerful predictor of later cognitive and academic outcomes, it is not the only important predictor of later outcome.
